117	def _represent_mixin_as_column(col, name, new_cols, mixin_cols, exclude_classes=()):
118	    """Carry out processing needed to serialize ``col`` in an output table
119	    consisting purely of plain ``Column`` or ``MaskedColumn`` columns.  This
120	    relies on the object determine if any transformation is required and may
121	    depend on the ``serialize_method`` and ``serialize_context`` context
122	    variables.  For instance a ``MaskedColumn`` may be stored directly to
123	    FITS, but can also be serialized as separate data and mask columns.
124	
125	    This function builds up a list of plain columns in the ``new_cols`` arg (which
126	    is passed as a persistent list).  This includes both plain columns from the
127	    original table and plain columns that represent data from serialized columns
128	    (e.g. ``jd1`` and ``jd2`` arrays from a ``Time`` column).
129	
130	    For serialized columns the ``mixin_cols`` dict is updated with required
131	    attributes and information to subsequently reconstruct the table.
132	
133	    Table mixin columns are always serialized and get represented by one
134	    or more data columns.  In earlier versions of the code *only* mixin
135	    columns were serialized, hence the use within this code of "mixin"
136	    to imply serialization.  Starting with version 3.1, the non-mixin
137	    ``MaskedColumn`` can also be serialized.
138	    """
139	    obj_attrs = col.info._represent_as_dict()
140	
141	    # If serialization is not required (see function docstring above)
142	    # or explicitly specified as excluded, then treat as a normal column.
143	    if not obj_attrs or col.__class__ in exclude_classes:
144	        new_cols.append(col)
145	        return
146	
147	    # Subtlety here is handling mixin info attributes.  The basic list of such
148	    # attributes is: 'name', 'unit', 'dtype', 'format', 'description', 'meta'.
149	    # - name: handled directly [DON'T store]
150	    # - unit: DON'T store if this is a parent attribute
151	    # - dtype: captured in plain Column if relevant [DON'T store]
152	    # - format: possibly irrelevant but settable post-object creation [DO store]
153	    # - description: DO store
154	    # - meta: DO store
155	    info = {}
156	    for attr, nontrivial in (
157	        ("unit", lambda x: x is not None and x != ""),
158	        ("format", lambda x: x is not None),
159	        ("description", lambda x: x is not None),
160	        ("meta", lambda x: x),
161	    ):
162	        col_attr = getattr(col.info, attr)
163	        if nontrivial(col_attr):
164	            info[attr] = col_attr
165	
166	    # Find column attributes that have the same length as the column itself.
167	    # These will be stored in the table as new columns (aka "data attributes").
168	    # Examples include SkyCoord.ra (what is typically considered the data and is
169	    # always an array) and Skycoord.obs_time (which can be a scalar or an
170	    # array).
171	    data_attrs = [
172	        key
173	        for key, value in obj_attrs.items()
174	        if getattr(value, "shape", ())[:1] == col.shape[:1]
175	    ]
176	
177	    for data_attr in data_attrs:
178	        data = obj_attrs[data_attr]
179	
180	        # New column name combines the old name and attribute
181	        # (e.g. skycoord.ra, skycoord.dec).unless it is the primary data
182	        # attribute for the column (e.g. value for Quantity or data for
183	        # MaskedColumn).  For primary data, we attempt to store any info on
184	        # the format, etc., on the column, but not for ancillary data (e.g.,
185	        # no sense to use a float format for a mask).
186	        is_primary = data_attr == col.info._represent_as_dict_primary_data
187	        if is_primary:
188	            new_name = name
189	            new_info = info
190	        else:
191	            new_name = name + "." + data_attr
192	            new_info = {}
193	
194	        if not has_info_class(data, MixinInfo):
195	            col_cls = (
196	                MaskedColumn
197	                if (
198	                    hasattr(data, "mask")
199	                    and np.any(data.mask != np.zeros((), data.mask.dtype))
200	                )
201	                else Column
202	            )
203	            data = col_cls(data, name=new_name, **new_info)
204	            if is_primary:
205	                # Don't store info in the __serialized_columns__ dict for this column
206	                # since this is redundant with info stored on the new column.
207	                info = {}
208	
209	        # Recurse. If this is anything that needs further serialization (i.e.,
210	        # a Mixin column, a structured Column, a MaskedColumn for which mask is
211	        # stored, etc.), it will define obj_attrs[new_name]. Otherwise, it will
212	        # just add to new_cols and all we have to do is to link to the new name.
213	        _represent_mixin_as_column(data, new_name, new_cols, obj_attrs)
214	        obj_attrs[data_attr] = SerializedColumn(
215	            obj_attrs.pop(new_name, {"name": new_name})
216	        )

219	    # and store whatever remains.
220	    for attr in col.info.attrs_from_parent:
221	        if attr in info:
222	            del info[attr]

224	        obj_attrs["__info__"] = info

226	    # Store the fully qualified class name
227	    if not isinstance(col, SerializedColumn):
228	        obj_attrs.setdefault("__class__", col.__module__ + "." + col.__class__.__name__)

233	def represent_mixins_as_columns(tbl, exclude_classes=()):
234	    """Represent input Table ``tbl`` using only `~astropy.table.Column`
235	    or  `~astropy.table.MaskedColumn` objects.
236	
237	    This function represents any mixin columns like `~astropy.time.Time` in
238	    ``tbl`` to one or more plain ``~astropy.table.Column`` objects and returns
239	    a new Table.  A single mixin column may be split into multiple column
240	    components as needed for fully representing the column.  This includes the
241	    possibility of recursive splitting, as shown in the example below.  The
242	    new column names are formed as ``<column_name>.<component>``, e.g.
243	    ``sc.ra`` for a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` column named ``sc``.
244	
245	    In addition to splitting columns, this function updates the table ``meta``
246	    dictionary to include a dict named ``__serialized_columns__`` which provides
247	    additional information needed to construct the original mixin columns from
248	    the split columns.
249	
250	    This function is used by astropy I/O when writing tables to ECSV, FITS,
251	    HDF5 formats.
252	
253	    Note that if the table does not include any mixin columns then the original
254	    table is returned with no update to ``meta``.
255	
256	    Parameters
257	    ----------
258	    tbl : `~astropy.table.Table` or subclass
259	        Table to represent mixins as Columns
260	    exclude_classes : tuple of class
261	        Exclude any mixin columns which are instannces of any classes in the tuple
262	
263	    Returns
264	    -------
265	    tbl : `~astropy.table.Table`
266	        New Table with updated columns, or else the original input ``tbl``
267	
268	    Examples
269	    --------
270	    >>> from astropy.table import Table, represent_mixins_as_columns
271	    >>> from astropy.time import Time
272	    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
273	
274	    >>> x = [100.0, 200.0]
275	    >>> obstime = Time([1999.0, 2000.0], format='jyear')
276	    >>> sc = SkyCoord([1, 2], [3, 4], unit='deg', obstime=obstime)
277	    >>> tbl = Table([sc, x], names=['sc', 'x'])
278	    >>> represent_mixins_as_columns(tbl)
279	    <Table length=2>
280	     sc.ra   sc.dec sc.obstime.jd1 sc.obstime.jd2    x
281	      deg     deg
282	    float64 float64    float64        float64     float64
283	    ------- ------- -------------- -------------- -------
284	        1.0     3.0      2451180.0          -0.25   100.0
285	        2.0     4.0      2451545.0            0.0   200.0
286	
287	    """
288	    # Dict of metadata for serializing each column, keyed by column name.
289	    # Gets filled in place by _represent_mixin_as_column().
290	    mixin_cols = {}
291	
292	    # List of columns for the output table.  For plain Column objects
293	    # this will just be the original column object.
294	    new_cols = []
295	
296	    # Go through table columns and represent each column as one or more
297	    # plain Column objects (in new_cols) + metadata (in mixin_cols).
298	    for col in tbl.itercols():
299	        _represent_mixin_as_column(
300	            col, col.info.name, new_cols, mixin_cols, exclude_classes=exclude_classes
301	        )
302	
303	    # If no metadata was created then just return the original table.
304	    if mixin_cols:
305	        meta = deepcopy(tbl.meta)
306	        meta["__serialized_columns__"] = mixin_cols
307	        out = Table(new_cols, meta=meta, copy=False)
308	    else:
309	        out = tbl
310	
311	    for col in out.itercols():
312	        if not isinstance(col, Column) and col.__class__ not in exclude_classes:
313	            # This catches columns for which info has not been set up right and
314	            # therefore were not converted. See the corresponding test in
315	            # test_mixin.py for an example.
316	            raise TypeError(
317	                "failed to represent column "
318	                f"{col.info.name!r} ({col.__class__.__name__}) as one "
319	                "or more Column subclasses. This looks like a mixin class "
320	                "that does not have the correct _represent_as_dict() method "
321	                "in the class `info` attribute."
322	            )
323	
324	    return out

327	def _construct_mixin_from_obj_attrs_and_info(obj_attrs, info):
328	    # If this is a supported class then import the class and run
329	    # the _construct_from_col method.  Prevent accidentally running
330	    # untrusted code by only importing known astropy classes.
331	    cls_full_name = obj_attrs.pop("__class__", None)
332	    if cls_full_name is None:
333	        # We're dealing with a SerializedColumn holding columns, stored in
334	        # obj_attrs. For this case, info holds the name (and nothing else).
335	        mixin = SerializedColumn(obj_attrs)
336	        mixin.info.name = info["name"]
337	        return mixin
338	
339	    # We translate locally created skyoffset frames and treat all
340	    # built-in frames as known.
341	    if cls_full_name.startswith("abc.SkyOffset"):
342	        cls_full_name = "astropy.coordinates.SkyOffsetFrame"
343	    elif (
344	        cls_full_name not in __construct_mixin_classes
345	        and not cls_full_name.startswith("astropy.coordinates.builtin_frames")
346	    ):
347	        raise ValueError(f"unsupported class for construct {cls_full_name}")
348	
349	    mod_name, _, cls_name = cls_full_name.rpartition(".")
350	    module = import_module(mod_name)
351	    cls = getattr(module, cls_name)
352	    for attr, value in info.items():
353	        if attr in cls.info.attrs_from_parent:
354	            obj_attrs[attr] = value
355	    mixin = cls.info._construct_from_dict(obj_attrs)
356	    for attr, value in info.items():
357	        if attr not in obj_attrs:
358	            setattr(mixin.info, attr, value)

362	class _TableLite(OrderedDict):
363	    """
364	    Minimal table-like object for _construct_mixin_from_columns.  This allows
365	    manipulating the object like a Table but without the actual overhead
366	    for a full Table.
367	
368	    More pressing, there is an issue with constructing MaskedColumn, where the
369	    encoded Column components (data, mask) are turned into a MaskedColumn.
370	    When this happens in a real table then all other columns are immediately
371	    Masked and a warning is issued. This is not desirable.
372	    """
373	
374	    def add_column(self, col, index=0):
375	        colnames = self.colnames
376	        self[col.info.name] = col
377	        for ii, name in enumerate(colnames):
378	            if ii >= index:
379	                self.move_to_end(name)
380

382	    def colnames(self):
383	        return list(self.keys())
384	
385	    def itercols(self):

389	def _construct_mixin_from_columns(new_name, obj_attrs, out):
390	    data_attrs_map = {}
391	    for name, val in obj_attrs.items():
392	        if isinstance(val, SerializedColumn):
393	            # A SerializedColumn can just link to a serialized column using a name
394	            # (e.g., time.jd1), or itself be a mixin (e.g., coord.obstime).  Note
395	            # that in principle a mixin could have include a column called 'name',
396	            # hence we check whether the value is actually a string (see gh-13232).
397	            if "name" in val and isinstance(val["name"], str):
398	                data_attrs_map[val["name"]] = name
399	            else:
400	                out_name = f"{new_name}.{name}"
401	                _construct_mixin_from_columns(out_name, val, out)
402	                data_attrs_map[out_name] = name
403	
404	    for name in data_attrs_map.values():
405	        del obj_attrs[name]
406	
407	    # The order of data_attrs_map may not match the actual order, as it is set
408	    # by the yaml description.  So, sort names by position in the serialized table.
409	    # Keep the index of the first column, so we can insert the new one there later.
410	    names = sorted(data_attrs_map, key=out.colnames.index)
411	    idx = out.colnames.index(names[0])
412	
413	    # Name is the column name in the table (e.g. "coord.ra") and
414	    # data_attr is the object attribute name  (e.g. "ra").  A different
415	    # example would be a formatted time object that would have (e.g.)
416	    # "time_col" and "value", respectively.
417	    for name in names:
418	        obj_attrs[data_attrs_map[name]] = out[name]
419	        del out[name]
420	
421	    info = obj_attrs.pop("__info__", {})
422	    if len(names) == 1:
423	        # col is the first and only serialized column; in that case, use info
424	        # stored on the column. First step is to get that first column which
425	        # has been moved from `out` to `obj_attrs` above.
426	        col = obj_attrs[data_attrs_map[name]]
427	
428	        # Now copy the relevant attributes
429	        for attr, nontrivial in (
430	            ("unit", lambda x: x not in (None, "")),
431	            ("format", lambda x: x is not None),
432	            ("description", lambda x: x is not None),
433	            ("meta", lambda x: x),
434	        ):
435	            col_attr = getattr(col.info, attr)
436	            if nontrivial(col_attr):
437	                info[attr] = col_attr
438	
439	    info["name"] = new_name
440	    col = _construct_mixin_from_obj_attrs_and_info(obj_attrs, info)
441	    out.add_column(col, index=idx)

444	def _construct_mixins_from_columns(tbl):
445	    if "__serialized_columns__" not in tbl.meta:
446	        return tbl
447	
448	    meta = tbl.meta.copy()
449	    mixin_cols = meta.pop("__serialized_columns__")
450	
451	    out = _TableLite(tbl.columns)
452	
453	    for new_name, obj_attrs in mixin_cols.items():
454	        _construct_mixin_from_columns(new_name, obj_attrs, out)
455	
456	    # If no quantity subclasses are in the output then output as Table.
457	    # For instance ascii.read(file, format='ecsv') doesn't specify an
458	    # output class and should return the minimal table class that
459	    # represents the table file.
460	    has_quantities = any(isinstance(col.info, QuantityInfo) for col in out.itercols())
461	    out_cls = QTable if has_quantities else Table
462	
463	    return out_cls(list(out.values()), names=out.colnames, copy=False, meta=meta)

5	Mixin Columns
6	*************
7	
8	``astropy`` tables support the concept of "mixin columns", which
9	allows integration of appropriate non-|Column| based class objects within a
10	|Table| object. These mixin column objects are not converted in any way but are
11	used natively.
12	
13	The available built-in mixin column classes are:
14	
15	- |Quantity| and subclasses
16	- |SkyCoord| and coordinate frame classes
17	- |Time| and :class:`~astropy.time.TimeDelta`
18	- :class:`~astropy.coordinates.EarthLocation`
19	- `~astropy.table.NdarrayMixin`
20	
21	Basic Example
22	=============
23	
24	.. EXAMPLE START: Using Mixin Columns in Tables
25	
26	As an example we can create a table and add a time column::
27	
28	  >>> from astropy.table import Table
29	  >>> from astropy.time import Time
30	  >>> t = Table()
31	  >>> t['index'] = [1, 2]
32	  >>> t['time'] = Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
33	  >>> print(t)
34	  index           time
35	  ----- -----------------------
36	      1 2001-01-02T12:34:56.000
37	      2 2001-02-03T00:01:02.000
38	
39	The important point here is that the ``time`` column is a bona fide |Time|
40	object::
41	
42	  >>> t['time']
43	  <Time object: scale='utc' format='isot' value=['2001-01-02T12:34:56.000' '2001-02-03T00:01:02.000']>
44	  >>> t['time'].mjd  # doctest: +FLOAT_CMP
45	  array([51911.52425926, 51943.00071759])
46	
47	.. EXAMPLE END
48	
49	.. _quantity_and_qtable:
50	
51	Quantity and QTable
52	===================
53	
54	The ability to natively handle |Quantity| objects within a table makes it more
55	convenient to manipulate tabular data with units in a natural and robust way.
56	However, this feature introduces an ambiguity because data with a unit
57	(e.g., from a FITS binary table) can be represented as either a |Column| with a
58	``unit`` attribute or as a |Quantity| object. In order to cleanly resolve this
59	ambiguity, ``astropy`` defines a minor variant of the |Table| class called
60	|QTable|. The |QTable| class is exactly the same as |Table| except that
61	|Quantity| is the default for any data column with a defined unit.
62	
63	If you take advantage of the |Quantity| infrastructure in your analysis, then
64	|QTable| is the preferred way to create tables with units. If instead you use
65	table column units more as a descriptive label, then the plain |Table| class is
66	probably the best class to use.
67	
68	Example
69	-------
70	
71	.. EXAMPLE START: Using Quantity Columns and QTables
72	
73	To illustrate these concepts we first create a standard |Table| where we supply
74	as input a |Time| object and a |Quantity| object with units of ``m / s``. In
75	this case the quantity is converted to a |Column| (which has a ``unit``
76	attribute but does not have all of the features of a |Quantity|)::
77	
78	  >>> import astropy.units as u
79	  >>> t = Table()
80	  >>> t['index'] = [1, 2]
81	  >>> t['time'] = Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
82	  >>> t['velocity'] = [3, 4] * u.m / u.s
83	
84	  >>> print(t)
85	  index           time          velocity
86	                                 m / s
87	  ----- ----------------------- --------
88	      1 2001-01-02T12:34:56.000      3.0
89	      2 2001-02-03T00:01:02.000      4.0
90	
91	  >>> type(t['velocity'])
92	  <class 'astropy.table.column.Column'>
93	
94	  >>> t['velocity'].unit
95	  Unit("m / s")
96	
97	  >>> (t['velocity'] ** 2).unit  # WRONG because Column is not smart about unit
98	  Unit("m / s")
99	
100	So instead let's do the same thing using a |QTable|::
101	
102	  >>> from astropy.table import QTable
103	
104	  >>> qt = QTable()
105	  >>> qt['index'] = [1, 2]
106	  >>> qt['time'] = Time(['2001-01-02T12:34:56', '2001-02-03T00:01:02'])
107	  >>> qt['velocity'] = [3, 4] * u.m / u.s
108	
109	The ``velocity`` column is now a |Quantity| and behaves accordingly::
110	
111	  >>> type(qt['velocity'])
112	  <class 'astropy.units.quantity.Quantity'>
113	
114	  >>> qt['velocity'].unit
115	  Unit("m / s")
116	
117	  >>> (qt['velocity'] ** 2).unit  # GOOD!
118	  Unit("m2 / s2")
119	
120	You can conveniently convert |Table| to |QTable| and vice-versa::
121	
122	  >>> qt2 = QTable(t)
123	  >>> type(qt2['velocity'])
124	  <class 'astropy.units.quantity.Quantity'>
125	
126	  >>> t2 = Table(qt2)
127	  >>> type(t2['velocity'])
128	  <class 'astropy.table.column.Column'>
129	
130	.. Note::
131	
132	   To summarize: the **only** difference between `~astropy.table.QTable` and
133	   `~astropy.table.Table` is the behavior when adding a column that has a
134	   specified unit. With `~astropy.table.QTable` such a column is always
135	   converted to a `~astropy.units.Quantity` object before being added to the
136	   table. Likewise if a unit is specified for an existing unit-less
137	   `~astropy.table.Column` in a `~astropy.table.QTable`, then the column is
138	   converted to `~astropy.units.Quantity`.
139	
140	   The converse is that if you add a `~astropy.units.Quantity` column to an
141	   ordinary `~astropy.table.Table` then it gets converted to an ordinary
142	   `~astropy.table.Column` with the corresponding ``unit`` attribute.
143	
144	.. attention::
145	
146	   When a column of ``int`` ``dtype`` is converted to `~astropy.units.Quantity`,
147	   its ``dtype`` is converted to ``float``.
148	
149	   For example, for a quality flag column of ``int``, if it is
150	   assigned with the :ref:`dimensionless unit <doc_dimensionless_unit>`, it will still
151	   be converted to ``float``. Therefore such columns typically should not be
152	   assigned with any unit.
153	
154	.. EXAMPLE END
155	
156	.. _mixin_attributes:
157	
158	Mixin Attributes
159	================
160	
161	The usual column attributes ``name``, ``dtype``, ``unit``, ``format``, and
162	``description`` are available in any mixin column via the ``info`` property::
163	
164	  >>> qt['velocity'].info.name
165	  'velocity'
166	
167	This ``info`` property is a key bit of glue that allows a non-|Column| object
168	to behave much like a |Column|.
169	
170	The same ``info`` property is also available in standard
171	`~astropy.table.Column` objects. These ``info`` attributes like
172	``t['a'].info.name`` refer to the direct `~astropy.table.Column`
173	attribute (e.g., ``t['a'].name``) and can be used interchangeably.
174	Likewise in a `~astropy.units.Quantity` object, ``info.dtype``
175	attribute refers to the native ``dtype`` attribute of the object.
176	
177	.. Note::
178	
179	   When writing generalized code that handles column objects which
180	   might be mixin columns, you must *always* use the ``info``
181	   property to access column attributes.
182	
183	.. _details_and_caveats:
184	
185	Details and Caveats
186	===================
187	
188	Most common table operations behave as expected when mixin columns are part of
189	the table. However, there are limitations in the current implementation.
190	
191	**Adding or inserting a row**
192	
193	Adding or inserting a row works as expected only for mixin classes that are
194	mutable (data can be changed internally) and that have an ``insert()`` method.
195	Adding rows to a |Table| with |Quantity|, |Time| or |SkyCoord| columns does
196	work.
197	
198	**Masking**
199	
200	Masking of mixin columns is enabled by the |Masked| class. See
201	:ref:`utils-masked` for details.
202	
203	**Text table writing**
204	
205	Tables with mixin columns can be written out to file using the
206	`astropy.io.ascii` module, but the fast C-based writers are not available.
207	Instead, the pure-Python writers will be used. For writing tables with mixin
208	columns it is recommended to use the :ref:`ecsv_format`. This will fully
209	serialize the table data and metadata, allowing full "round-trip" of the table
210	when it is read back.
211	
212	**Binary table writing**
213	
214	Tables with mixin columns can be written to binary files using FITS, HDF5 and
215	Parquet formats. These can be read back to recover exactly the original |Table|
216	including mixin columns and metadata. See :ref:`table_io` for details.
217	
218	.. _mixin_protocol:
219	
220	Mixin Protocol
221	==============
222	
223	A key idea behind mixin columns is that any class which satisfies a specified
224	protocol can be used. That means many user-defined class objects which handle
225	array-like data can be used natively within a |Table|. The protocol is
226	relatively concise and requires that a class behave like a minimal ``numpy``
227	array with the following properties:
228	
229	- Contains array-like data.
230	- Implements ``__getitem__()`` to support getting data as a
231	  single item, slicing, or index array access.
232	- Has a ``shape`` attribute.
233	- Has a ``__len__()`` method for length.
234	- Has an ``info`` class descriptor which is an instance of a subclass of the
235	  :class:`astropy.utils.data_info.MixinInfo` class.
236	
237	The `Example: ArrayWrapper`_ section shows a minimal working example of a class
238	which can be used as a mixin column. A :class:`pandas.Series` object can
239	function as a mixin column as well.
240	
241	Other interesting possibilities for mixin columns include:
242	
243	- Columns which are dynamically computed as a function of other columns (AKA
244	  spreadsheet).
245	- Columns which are themselves a |Table| (i.e., nested tables). A `proof of
246	  concept <https://github.com/astropy/astropy/pull/3963>`_ is available.
247	
248	new_like() method
249	-----------------
250	
251	In order to support high-level operations like :func:`~astropy.table.join` and
252	:func:`~astropy.table.vstack`, a mixin class must provide a ``new_like()``
253	method in the ``info`` class descriptor. A key part of the functionality is to
254	ensure that the input column metadata are merged appropriately and that the
255	columns have consistent properties such as the shape.
256	
257	A mixin class that provides ``new_like()`` must also implement
258	``__setitem__()`` to support setting via a single item, slicing, or index
259	array.
260	
261	The ``new_like()`` method has the following signature::
262	
263	    def new_like(self, cols, length, metadata_conflicts='warn', name=None):
264	        """
265	        Return a new instance of this class which is consistent with the
266	        input ``cols`` and has ``length`` rows.
267	
268	        This is intended for creating an empty column object whose elements can
269	        be set in-place for table operations like join or vstack.
270	
271	        Parameters
272	        ----------
273	        cols : list
274	            List of input columns
275	        length : int
276	            Length of the output column object
277	        metadata_conflicts : {'warn', 'error', 'silent'}
278	            How to handle metadata conflicts
279	        name : str
280	            Output column name
281	
282	        Returns
283	        -------
284	        col : object
285	            New instance of this class consistent with ``cols``
286	        """
287	
288	Examples of this are found in the `~astropy.table.column.ColumnInfo` and
289	`~astropy.units.quantity.QuantityInfo` classes.
290	
291	
292	.. _arraywrapper_example:
293	
294	Example: ArrayWrapper
295	=====================
296	
297	The code listing below shows an example of a data container class which acts as
298	a mixin column class. This class is a wrapper around a |ndarray|. It is used in
299	the ``astropy`` mixin test suite and is fully compliant as a mixin column.
300	
301	::
302	
303	  from astropy.utils.data_info import ParentDtypeInfo
304	
305	  class ArrayWrapper:
306	      """
307	      Minimal mixin using a simple wrapper around a numpy array
308	      """
309	      info = ParentDtypeInfo()
310	
311	      def __init__(self, data):
312	          self.data = np.array(data)
313	          if 'info' in getattr(data, '__dict__', ()):
314	              self.info = data.info
315	
316	      def __getitem__(self, item):
317	          if isinstance(item, (int, np.integer)):
318	              out = self.data[item]
319	          else:
320	              out = self.__class__(self.data[item])
321	              if 'info' in self.__dict__:
322	                  out.info = self.info
323	          return out
324	
325	      def __setitem__(self, item, value):
326	          self.data[item] = value
327	
328	      def __len__(self):
329	          return len(self.data)
330	
331	      @property
332	      def dtype(self):
333	          return self.data.dtype
334	
335	      @property
336	      def shape(self):
337	          return self.data.shape
338	
339	      def __repr__(self):
340	          return f"<{self.__class__.__name__} name='{self.info.name}' data={self.data}>"
341	
342	.. _table_mixin_registry:
343	
344	Registering array-like objects as mixin columns
345	===============================================
346	
347	In some cases, you may want to directly add an array-like
348	object as a table column while maintaining the original object properties
349	(instead of the default conversion of the object to a `~astropy.table.Column`).
350	This is done by registering the object class as a mixin column and
351	defining a handler which allows `~astropy.table.Table` to treat that object
352	class as a mixin similar to the built-in mixin columns such as `~astropy.time.Time`
353	or `~astropy.units.quantity.Quantity`.
354	
355	This can be done for data classes that are defined in third-party packages and which
356	you have no control over. As an example, we define a class
357	that is not numpy-like and stores the data in a private attribute::
358	
359	    >>> import numpy as np
360	    >>> class ExampleDataClass:
361	    ...     def __init__(self):
362	    ...         self._data = np.array([0, 1, 3, 4], dtype=float)
363	
364	By default, the outcome of setting a column using this class is not helpful::
365	
366	    >>> t = Table([np.arange(4)], names=["index"])
367	    >>> t['data'] = ExampleDataClass()
368	    >>> t
369	    <Table length=4>
370	    index                         data
371	    int64                        object
372	    ----- -------------------------------------...-
373	        0 <__main__.ExampleDataClass object at ...>
374	        1 <__main__.ExampleDataClass object at ...>
375	        2 <__main__.ExampleDataClass object at ...>
376	        3 <__main__.ExampleDataClass object at ...>
377	
378	What happened is that the instance is seen as a scalar object, and a
379	|Column| with ``dtype=object`` is created, which has the same entry for
380	each row. The same would happen if, e.g., you set ``t['data'] = None``.
381	
382	However, you can create a function (or 'handler') which takes
383	an instance of the data class you want to have automatically
384	handled and turns it into a mixin column::
385	
386	    >>> from astropy.table.table_helpers import ArrayWrapper
387	    >>> def handle_example_data_class(obj):
388	    ...     return ArrayWrapper(obj._data)
389	
390	You can then register this by providing the fully qualified name
391	of the class and the handler function::
392	
393	    >>> from astropy.table.mixins.registry import register_mixin_handler
394	    >>> register_mixin_handler('__main__.ExampleDataClass', handle_example_data_class)
395	    >>> t['data'] = ExampleDataClass()
396	    >>> t
397	    <Table length=4>
398	    index   data
399	    int64 float64
400	    ----- -------
401	        0     0.0
402	        1     1.0
403	        2     3.0
404	        3     4.0
405	
406	.. testcleanup::
407	
408	    >>> from astropy.table.mixins.registry import _handlers
409	    >>> del _handlers['__main__.ExampleDataClass']
410	
411	Because we defined the data class as part of the example
412	above, the fully qualified name starts with ``__main__``,
413	but for a class in a third-party package, this might look
414	like ``package.Class`` for example.

"""
Support round-tripping sunpy coordinate frames through astropy table I/O.

Astropy's unified table write/read support (e.g., FITS, ECSV, HDF5 and
Parquet) serializes mixin columns such as `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` —
including their frame attributes, which for sunpy frames can themselves be
coordinate frames (e.g., the ``observer`` of `~sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective`).
Writing such a table records for every object the fully qualified name of its
class.  When the table is read back, astropy refuses to instantiate any class
that is not on a safeguard allow list
(``astropy.table.serialize.__construct_mixin_classes``), which contains only
astropy's own built-in classes, so sunpy frames cannot be rebuilt by default.

Registering sunpy's coordinate frame classes on that allow list enables
catalogues holding solar coordinates to be archived and restored without
losing their scientific meaning.
"""

from astropy.table import serialize as _serialize

from sunpy import log
from .frames import SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame

__all__ = ["register_sunpy_frame_classes"]


def _iter_sunpy_frame_classes():
    """
    Walk the `~sunpy.coordinates.frames.SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame` class tree
    and yield every sunpy-defined subclass discovered (including abstract
    base classes, which is harmless if they never appear in a table).
    """
    seen = set()
    pending = [SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame]
    while pending:
        cls = pending.pop()
        if cls in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(cls)
        yield cls
        pending.extend(cls.__subclasses__())


def _constructible_class_name(cls):
    """Return the fully qualified class name used by astropy's serializer."""
    return f"{cls.__module__}.{cls.__name__}"


def register_sunpy_frame_classes():
    """
    Extend astropy's table-serialization allow list with sunpy's coordinate
    frame classes so that tables containing them can be read back.

    This function is idempotent.  If astropy's serialization internals have
    changed such that the allow list no longer exists, registration is
    skipped with a debug message rather than failing the sunpy import.
    """
    construct_mixin_classes = getattr(_serialize, "__construct_mixin_classes", None)
    if construct_mixin_classes is None:
        log.debug(
            "astropy.table.serialize has no __construct_mixin_classes allow list; "
            "tables containing sunpy coordinates may not round-trip through astropy table I/O."
        )
        return

    new_names = [
        _constructible_class_name(cls)
        for cls in _iter_sunpy_frame_classes()
        if _constructible_class_name(cls) not in construct_mixin_classes
    ]
    if new_names:
        _serialize.__construct_mixin_classes = tuple(construct_mixin_classes) + tuple(new_names)
        log.debug(
            "Registered sunpy coordinate frames with astropy table serialization: %s",
            new_names,
        )

"""
Support round-tripping sunpy coordinate frames through astropy table I/O.

Astropy's unified table write/read support (e.g., FITS, ECSV, HDF5 and
Parquet) serializes mixin columns such as `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` —
including their frame attributes, which for sunpy frames can themselves be
coordinate frames (e.g., the ``observer`` of `~sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective`).
Writing such a table records for every object the fully qualified name of its
class, and scalar (non-array) attribute values are stored directly in the
table metadata using astropy's YAML machinery.  On reading, astropy only
rebuilds objects of classes that it knows about:

* `astropy.table.serialize` refuses to instantiate any class that is not on
  its safeguard allow list (``__construct_mixin_classes``), which contains
  only astropy's own built-in classes.
* `astropy.io.misc.yaml` has doc-tag representers/constructors only for
  classes in the public ``astropy.coordinates`` API, so scalar sunpy frames
  embedded in metadata can neither be dumped nor loaded.

Registering sunpy's coordinate frame classes with both pieces of machinery
enables catalogues holding solar coordinates to be archived and restored
without losing their scientific meaning.
"""

from astropy.io.misc import yaml as _astropy_yaml
from astropy.table import serialize as _serialize

from sunpy import log
from .frames import SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame

__all__ = ["register_sunpy_frame_classes"]


def _iter_sunpy_frame_classes():
    """
    Walk the `~sunpy.coordinates.frames.SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame` class tree
    and yield every sunpy-defined subclass discovered (including abstract
    base classes, which is harmless if they never appear in a table).
    """
    seen = set()
    pending = [SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame]
    while pending:
        cls = pending.pop()
        if cls in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(cls)
        yield cls
        pending.extend(cls.__subclasses__())


def _qualified_class_name(cls):
    """Return the fully qualified class name used by astropy's serializer."""
    return f"{cls.__module__}.{cls.__name__}"


def _sunpy_frame_yaml_tag(cls):
    """Return the YAML tag used to embed scalar frame objects in metadata."""
    return f"!{_qualified_class_name(cls)}"


def _frame_representer(tag):
    """
    Mirror `astropy.io.misc.yaml._quantity_representer` for coordinate frames:
    dump the frame via its ``info._represent_as_dict()`` under ``tag``.
    """

    def representer(dumper, obj):
        out = obj.info._represent_as_dict()
        return dumper.represent_mapping(tag, out)

    return representer


def _frame_constructor(cls):
    """
    Mirror `astropy.io.misc.yaml._quantity_constructor` for coordinate frames:
    rebuild the frame via ``cls.info._construct_from_dict()``.
    """

    def constructor(loader, node):
        mapping = loader.construct_mapping(node)
        return cls.info._construct_from_dict(mapping)

    return constructor


def _register_construct_mixin_classes():
    """
    Allow `astropy.table.serialize` to rebuild sunpy frames appearing as
    table columns or as vector-valued frame attributes.
    """
    construct_mixin_classes = getattr(_serialize, "__construct_mixin_classes", None)
    if construct_mixin_classes is None:
        log.debug(
            "astropy.table.serialize has no __construct_mixin_classes allow list; "
            "tables containing sunpy coordinates may not round-trip through astropy table I/O."
        )
        return []

    new_names = [
        _qualified_class_name(cls)
        for cls in _iter_sunpy_frame_classes()
        if _qualified_class_name(cls) not in construct_mixin_classes
    ]
    if new_names:
        _serialize.__construct_mixin_classes = tuple(construct_mixin_classes) + tuple(new_names)
    return new_names


def _register_yaml_frame_encodings():
    """
    Allow scalar sunpy frames embedded in table metadata to be dumped to and
    constructed from YAML by `astropy.io.misc.yaml` (used by the FITS, ECSV,
    HDF5 and Parquet table readers and writers).
    """
    new_tags = []
    for cls in _iter_sunpy_frame_classes():
        if cls not in _astropy_yaml.AstropyDumper.yaml_multi_representers:
            _astropy_yaml.AstropyDumper.add_multi_representer(
                cls, _frame_representer(_sunpy_frame_yaml_tag(cls))

        tag = _sunpy_frame_yaml_tag(cls)
        if tag not in _astropy_yaml.AstropyLoader.yaml_constructors:
            _astropy_yaml.AstropyLoader.add_constructor(tag, _frame_constructor(cls))
            new_tags.append(tag)
    return new_tags


def register_sunpy_frame_classes():
    """
    Extend astropy's table-serialization machinery so that tables containing
    sunpy coordinate frames can be written to and read back from files.

    This function is idempotent.  If astropy's serialization internals have
    changed such that the allow list no longer exists, registration is
    skipped with a debug message rather than failing the sunpy import.
    """

    new_tags = _register_yaml_frame_encodings()

        log.debug(
            "Registered sunpy coordinate frames with astropy table serialization: "
            "%d constructible classes, %d YAML tags.",
            len(new_names),
            len(new_tags),

"""
Tests for round-tripping sunpy coordinate objects through astropy's unified
table write/read support (FITS and ECSV).
"""

import numpy as np
import pytest

import astropy.units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
from astropy.table import QTable
from astropy.time import Time

from sunpy.coordinates import HeliographicStonyhurst, Helioprojective


def _example_helioprojective_skycoord(n=5):
    """A Helioprojective coordinate sequence with a per-row observer."""
    times = Time(["2025-02-14T08:00:00", "2025-02-15T08:00:00", "2025-02-16T08:00:00",
                  "2025-02-17T08:00:00", "2025-02-18T08:00:00"])[:n]
    observer = HeliographicStonyhurst(
        np.linspace(7.0, 13.0, n) * u.deg,
        np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, n) * u.deg,
        np.linspace(0.74, 0.82, n) * u.AU,
        obstime=times,
    )
    frame = Helioprojective(observer=observer, obstime=times)
    return SkyCoord(
        np.linspace(-640.0, 675.0, n) * u.arcsec,
        np.linspace(105.0, -95.0, n) * u.arcsec,
        frame=frame,
    )


def _example_scalar_observer_skycoord(n=3):
    """A Helioprojective coordinate sequence with a single shared observer."""
    observer = HeliographicStonyhurst(20 * u.deg, 2 * u.deg, 0.99 * u.AU,
                                      obstime=Time("2026-01-01T00:00:00"))
    frame = Helioprojective(observer=observer, obstime=Time("2026-01-01T00:00:00"),
                            rsun=696000 * u.km)
    return SkyCoord(np.linspace(-100.0, 100.0, n) * u.arcsec,
                    np.linspace(-50.0, 50.0, n) * u.arcsec,
                    frame=frame)


def _assert_same_coordinate(before, after):
    assert before.shape == after.shape
    assert before.is_equivalent_frame(after)
    offset = before.separation(after).to_value(u.arcsec)
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(offset))
    assert np.max(np.abs(offset)) < 1e-8


@pytest.mark.parametrize("table_format", ["fits", "ascii.ecsv"])
def test_skycoord_table_round_trip_vector_observer(tmp_path, table_format):
    """A catalogue column of Helioprojective coordinates with a per-row
    observer must survive archiving and reloading."""
    table = QTable()
    table["sequence"] = np.arange(5, dtype=np.int64)
    table["position"] = _example_helioprojective_skycoord()

    path = tmp_path / "catalogue"
    table.write(path, format=table_format)
    restored = QTable.read(path, format=table_format)

    assert restored.colnames == table.colnames
    assert np.array_equal(restored["sequence"], table["sequence"])
    _assert_same_coordinate(table["position"], restored["position"])


@pytest.mark.parametrize("table_format", ["fits", "ascii.ecsv"])
def test_skycoord_table_round_trip_scalar_observer(tmp_path, table_format):
    """The scalar-observer case stores the observer in the table metadata,
    which exercises a different serialization code path."""
    table = QTable()
    table["position"] = _example_scalar_observer_skycoord()

    path = tmp_path / "catalogue"
    table.write(path, format=table_format)
    restored = QTable.read(path, format=table_format)

    _assert_same_coordinate(table["position"], restored["position"])
    assert restored["position"].frame.rsun == 696000 * u.km


@pytest.mark.parametrize("table_format", ["fits", "ascii.ecsv"])
def test_bare_sunpy_frame_table_round_trip(tmp_path, table_format):
    """A bare sunpy frame (rather than a SkyCoord) is a valid table column
    and must also round-trip."""
    frame = HeliographicStonyhurst([5.0, 6.0, 7.0] * u.deg,
                                   [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0] * u.deg,
                                   [0.9, 0.91, 0.92] * u.AU,
                                   obstime=Time(["2026-02-01", "2026-02-02", "2026-02-03"]))
    table = QTable()
    table["coordinate"] = frame

    path = tmp_path / "catalogue"
    table.write(path, format=table_format)
    restored = QTable.read(path, format=table_format)

    assert isinstance(restored["coordinate"], HeliographicStonyhurst)
    assert np.allclose(restored["coordinate"].lon.to_value(u.deg),
                       frame.lon.to_value(u.deg))
    assert np.allclose(restored["coordinate"].radius.to_value(u.AU),
                       frame.radius.to_value(u.AU))

Repaired. `python reproduce.py` now exits `0` with `status: post_fix_success`.

## Root cause

The catalogue stores a `SkyCoord` column in sunpy's `Helioprojective` frame, whose `observer` attribute is itself a sunpy `HeliographicStonyhurst` frame. Astropy archives all of this faithfully into the FITS header (`__serialized_columns__` YAML + data columns), but on reload it refused to rebuild the objects:

1. `astropy.table.serialize._construct_mixin_from_obj_attrs_and_info` only instantiates classes on a hard-coded allow list (`__construct_mixin_classes`) — astropy's own classes plus `astropy.coordinates.builtin_frames.*`. Any sunpy frame raised `ValueError: unsupported class for construct sunpy.coordinates.frames.HeliographicStonyhurst`, which the workflow caught and reported as an unusable catalogue.
2. A second, deeper gap: scalar (non-array) frame values are stored directly in the table's YAML metadata, and `astropy.io.misc.yaml` only registers representers/constructors for classes in the public `astropy.coordinates` API. So a *scalar* sunpy observer couldn't even be written. (I verified the astropy-native analogue — a scalar `EarthLocation` — does round-trip, confirming this is the missing third-party piece.)

## Fix (all under `source/`; workflow, fixtures, reproduction untouched)

- New private module `sunpy/coordinates/_table_serialization.py`: discovers every `SunPyBaseCoordinateFrame` subclass and registers it with both mechanisms — extends astropy's construct-mixin allow list, and adds YAML multi-representers/constructors to `AstropyDumper`/`AstropyLoader` mirroring astropy's own `_quantity_*` pattern. Registration is idempotent and logs a debug message instead of crashing if astropy's internals ever change.
- Hooked it at the end of `sunpy/coordinates/__init__.py:31-38`, after all frame modules are imported, so it runs whenever sunpy's coordinates are used.
- Added `sunpy/coordinates/tests/test_table_serialization.py` (6 tests: vector/scalar observer, bare frame column, FITS/ECSV).

## Verification

- `reproduce.py` exits `0`; exact recovery (`max separation = 0.0 arcsec`).
- Generalization checked beyond the supplied catalogue: vector and scalar observers; `SkyCoord` *and* bare-frame columns; `Helioprojective` (spherical and cartesian), `Heliocentric`, `HeliographicStonyhurst`, `HeliographicCarrington`, `HeliocentricInertial`, `GeocentricEarthEquatorial` (scalar `equinox` attribute); FITS, ECSV, and Parquet archives; single-row catalogues; custom `rsun` preserved.
- No regressions: `test_frames.py` 122 passed, plus `test_frameattributes`/`test_transformations` within a 263-pass run. Only pre-existing environment gaps remain (`hypothesis` not installed for two test modules; 12 `test_utils.py` errors about missing installed package metadata — both verified present on the untouched baseline).
